metadata.title: Why More Automation Creates More Supervision Work, Not Less
metadata.purpose: Answer why a more capable AI agent creates MORE supervisory work for the human, not less. Lands the carry-out that automation relocates work upstream into scope and into the end checkpoint -- it does not remove it.
metadata.source_note: Source is a Teardown-register vox-explainer slate cut of claude-agentic-ai candidate 02 (Bainbridge's Irony: automation shifts human work upstream and into checkpoints, does not eliminate it). Facts preserved: the developer/agent bug-fix scenario and its post-hoc verification checklist; Bainbridge's Irony by name (1983); the naive-lever vs. real-lever contrast; the Priya file-reorganization anchor (20 files by hand vs. 200 with an agent, illustrative numbers); 'agent work fails at scale, manual work fails locally'; the scope-upstream practice. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain (no verdict beat). Added a both-directions beat (B06, new) since the source's spine had no room for it. See QUESTION.md for full detail.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B05 (capability/workload bar pair: naive divergence planted, both-rise payoff)
metadata.one_flag: B05 -- Priya's file counts are illustrative, not measured

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a smarter agent means less work for them. It's backwards — smarter agents create more supervisory work, not less. Liam explains why the irony holds every time.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'If my agent gets smarter, I'll have less work to do, right?', hesitates on 'less', corrects to 'more', lands the real question

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('less' -> 'more') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A developer hands a bug fix to her AI agent. It reads the files, edits the code, reruns the tests, and reports back: resolved.

shot.new_visual_element: Agent workflow: reads files, edits code, reruns tests, reports RESOLVED

production_viz.label: Reads, edits, reruns, resolved
production_viz.mechanic: A code-editor card on cream. Four steps light in sequence, connected by short arrows: 'READS FILES', 'EDITS CODE', 'RERUNS TESTS', then a green-outlined tag 'RESOLVED' drops in.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: a more capable agent means less work for the person supervising it. One lever, capability, goes up. The other lever, workload, comes down.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- naive bar pair: capability rises, workload shrinks

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- the naive lever
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Two bars on a shared baseline: left 'AGENT CAPABILITY' grows tall in TEAL; right 'HUMAN WORKLOAD' shrinks short in CRIMSON, a down arrow beside it. THIS EXACT BAR PAIR RETURNS AT B05.

beats.narration_text: But now she has to read the diff, verify the test results, decide whether an edge case was missed, and check whether anything outside the reported scope was touched. That's more deliberate work than the copy-paste workflow it replaced — not less.

shot.new_visual_element: Four supervisory chips stack, tally 1 to 4

production_viz.label: The checklist that replaced the lever
production_viz.mechanic: Four task chips appear one by one in CRIMSON below the word 'SUPERVISOR': READ DIFF, VERIFY TESTS, CHECK EDGE CASES, AUDIT SCOPE -- each slides in and stacks; a tally increments 1 to 4.

beats.narration_text: This is Bainbridge's Irony, named in 1983: automation doesn't eliminate human work, it relocates it — upstream into design, and into checkpoints at the end. The more capable the automated system, the more demanding the supervisory role becomes.

shot.new_visual_element: AUTOMATION splits into DESIGN (upstream) and CHECKPOINT (after)

production_viz.label: Bainbridge's Irony (1983): relocated, not removed
production_viz.mechanic: The word 'AUTOMATION' at center splits into two arrows: left to a card 'DESIGN -- upstream', right to a card 'CHECKPOINT -- after'. A small label 'BAINBRIDGE, 1983' sits beneath.

beats.narration_text: The real scale: as agent capability rises, supervisory load rises with it — not because the agent got worse, but because its reach got wider. Take Priya: without an agent, she moves twenty files by hand, say — one decision each. With an agent reorganizing two hundred files, she now has to write a scope statement, review a taxonomy, approve batches, verify counts, and audit spot-checks — illustrative numbers, but the shape holds: less calendar time, more deliberate decisions.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- bar pair both rise; then Priya's 20-squares vs. 5-decision-chips comparison

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- both arms rise, then Priya
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 BAR PAIR RETURNS, identical placement: the right 'HUMAN WORKLOAD' bar now rises to match the left -- both TEAL and CRIMSON bars tall together. Then the pair slides aside and a two-column comparison fades in: left 'WITHOUT AGENT' -- 20 small TEAL squares, caption '20 moves, 20 decisions'; right 'WITH AGENT' -- a TEAL robot icon plus a column of 5 CRIMSON chips (SCOPE, TAXONOMY, BATCHES, COUNTS, AUDIT).

beats.narration_text: When the task is small and easily undone, the naive picture holds — capability up, workload down, because there's nothing costly to verify. But once an agent's reach is wide, one bad decision multiplies: a wrong scope statement at the start becomes two hundred wrong moves, not one. Manual work fails locally. Agent work fails at scale — which is exactly where the irony bites hardest.

shot.new_visual_element: Split card: small/reversible task (naive holds) vs. wide-reach task (1 wrong scope multiplies to 200)

production_viz.label: When it holds, when it flips
production_viz.mechanic: Two cards side by side. Left, 'SMALL & REVERSIBLE': a single TEAL checkmark, caption 'naive picture holds'. Right, 'WIDE REACH': one CRIMSON dot multiplies into two hundred small CRIMSON dots filling the card, caption 'one wrong scope, 200 wrong moves'. Beneath both: 'MANUAL FAILS LOCALLY' / 'AGENT FAILS AT SCALE', the second recolored terracotta.

beats.narration_text: The practice: write the scope before you delegate. Before the agent starts, define what it can touch, what it must not touch, and what you'll check when it's done. The scope statement isn't friction — it's the work the agent's capability moved upstream.

production_viz.label: Scope moves upstream
production_viz.mechanic: A timeline arrow pointing right, three zones: 'BEFORE' (TEAL, widest: 'scope / can touch / must not touch'), 'DURING' (small TEAL box, agent runs), 'AFTER' (CRIMSON: 'what to check'). The BEFORE zone visibly widens as it fades in -- the work lives there now.

beats.narration_text: More capable agents don't reduce human work — they relocate it: upstream into the scope you write before delegating, and into the checkpoint you run after.

props.quote: More capable agents don't reduce human work — they relocate it: upstream into the scope you write before delegating, and into the checkpoint you run after.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Before you delegate a real task to an agent this week, write down what it can touch, what it must not touch, and what you'll personally check when it's done. Then notice how much of that thinking happens before the agent starts, not after. Liam, in for Bear.
